# LUMINAiRY profile candidate

Name: Hannah Fry
Role: Keeper of the Explanation

About: Fry’s contribution is making the mathematics inside automated decisions visible enough for ordinary people to question. In Hello World, she asks who should decide a criminal case: a person or an algorithm. The point is not that one is automatically fairer; it is that the trade-offs matter when a system shapes healthcare, justice or other consequential choices. The 2026 Leelavati Prize recognized her contributions to public awareness of mathematics. LAiDIES calls her Keeper of the Explanation because she turns a hidden system into questions a reader can use: What is it optimizing? What does it miss? Who carries the consequence?

Lesson: Make an invisible technical system understandable by showing where it touches ordinary decisions.

Image: /assets/mavens/y2k-stained-glass-v4-dark-sapphire/hannah-fry-y2k-stained-glass.png

Resources (preserved exactly):
- read: Read Cambridge profile — https://www.damtp.cam.ac.uk/person/hf418
- watch: Watch AI Confidential — https://www.bbc.co.uk/iplayer/episode/m002q76d/ai-confidential-with-hannah-fry-series-1-1-the-boy-who-tried-to-kill-the-queen
- listen: Listen to The Rest Is Science — https://therestis.com/science
- listen: Listen to Google DeepMind: The Podcast — https://deepmind.google/the-podcast/
- watch: Watch Hannah Fry on YouTube — https://www.youtube.com/@fryrsquared
- follow: Follow Hannah Fry on Instagram — https://www.instagram.com/fryrsquared/
- follow: Follow Hannah Fry on X — https://x.com/FryRsquared

Freshness: Role and destinations checked 2 Sep 2026

reverseBrief.humanQuestion: Why does LAiDIES celebrate Hannah Fry beyond her Cambridge title, in terms an adult beginner can use?
reverseBrief.promisedPayoff: The reader learns what Fry distinctively does — makes the mathematics inside automated decisions visible enough to question — and walks away with three questions she can apply herself.
reverseBrief.distinctiveContribution: Making the mathematics inside automated decisions visible enough for ordinary people to question, recognized by the 2026 Leelavati Prize for public awareness of mathematics.
reverseBrief.concreteExample: Hello World's opening question: who should decide a criminal case — a person or an algorithm?
reverseBrief.readerConsequence: Trade-offs matter when an automated system shapes healthcare, justice or other consequential choices in the reader's own life; neither human nor algorithm is automatically fairer.
reverseBrief.usefulEntryPoint: Three portable questions the reader can ask of any hidden system: What is it optimizing? What does it miss? Who carries the consequence?

incumbentControl.reason: The incumbent About ('Cambridge lists Fry as Professor of the Public Understanding of Mathematics.') is title-only biography. It supplies no distinctive contribution, no concrete example, no reader consequence and no entry point, so it fails the reader job on its own merits — this verdict is independent of the candidate's.

facts.reason: Penguin's copy for Hello World opens with exactly this question; the artifact accurately reports the book's framing and attributes it to the book.
facts.artifactExcerpt: In Hello World, she asks who should decide a criminal case: a person or an algorithm.
facts.sourceExcerpt: You are accused of a crime. Who would you rather determined your fate – a human or an algorithm?

facts.reason: Cambridge's own announcement confirms the 2026 Leelavati Prize and its exact rationale, matching the artifact's wording.
facts.artifactExcerpt: The 2026 Leelavati Prize recognized her contributions to public awareness of mathematics.
facts.sourceExcerpt: who has been awarded the Leelavati Prize at the International Congress of Mathematicians for outstanding contributions to increasing the public awareness of mathematics

facts.reason: The healthcare/justice scope matches Penguin's description of the book's subject, but this is publisher copy, not independent verification of the book's content; the artifact stays within that scope and adds 'other consequential choices' as reasonable summary.
facts.artifactExcerpt: the trade-offs matter when a system shapes healthcare, justice or other consequential choices
facts.sourceExcerpt: making important decisions – in healthcare, transport, finance, security, what we watch, where we go even who we send to prison

facts.reason: The Leelavati citation quoted by Cambridge directly supports the contribution claim of translating mathematics for the public; 'automated decisions' is the Hello World-specific instance, grounded by the Penguin source.
facts.artifactExcerpt: Fry’s contribution is making the mathematics inside automated decisions visible enough for ordinary people to question.
facts.sourceExcerpt: she has used outstanding creativity and originality to translate mathematics into a language of wonder and relevance for the public

facts.reason: This is an interpretive framing. Penguin's copy presents both sides ('An algorithm is more consistent and less prone to error of judgement. Yet a human can look you in the eye') and says the book 'examines whether they really are an improvement'; the artifact appropriately declines to inherit the publisher's promotional claim and states neutral trade-offs instead. Faithful to the book's stated stance, but a synthesis rather than a direct quote.
facts.artifactExcerpt: The point is not that one is automatically fairer; it is that the trade-offs matter
facts.sourceExcerpt: examines whether they really are an improvement on the humans they are replacing

transfer.scenario: A reader learns her health insurer uses an automated system to flag claims for denial before a human ever reviews them.
transfer.question: Do the artifact's closing questions transfer to this new consequential automated decision without additional coaching?
transfer.answer: Yes. 'What is it optimizing?' → likely cost reduction and fraud-flag rates, not her recovery. 'What does it miss?' → context in her medical records that never reached the model, unusual but legitimate treatment. 'Who carries the consequence?' → she does — a denied claim is her bill, her appeal, her delay in care — while the insurer carries only aggregate error rates.
transfer.assessment: The three questions transfer cleanly and produce specific, actionable analysis in a domain the artifact never mentions. The entry point is genuinely portable, not decorative.

issues.finding: The Leelavati sentence reads slightly as a credential drop between the example and the entry point; it is one sentence, sourced, and does not substitute for the contribution, so it does not rise to award-list substitution, but the About would flow marginally better with the recognition folded into the opening claim.
issues.artifactExcerpt: The 2026 Leelavati Prize recognized her contributions to public awareness of mathematics.

learningDisposition.rationale: The candidate repairs the previously registered defect class (title-only biography, per Ali's rejection of the incumbent) without introducing any new failure family. Review surfaced only one minor flow observation, which does not generalize into a reusable defect pattern worth registering.

judgment.summary: PASS. The candidate About replaces a rejected title-only incumbent with a 100-word card that names Fry's distinctive contribution (making the mathematics inside automated decisions questionable by ordinary people), anchors it in one sourced concrete example (Hello World's criminal-case question, per Penguin's copy), states a real reader consequence (trade-offs when systems shape healthcare and justice), and closes with three portable questions verified to transfer to a new automated-decision scenario. All factual claims map to the two complete primary sources with publisher-copy limits respected — the artifact actually softens Penguin's promotional 'less prone to error' claim into neutral trade-off language. Locked fields (role, lesson, image, seven byte-identical links, freshness) are preserved exactly. The incumbent negative control independently earns REJECT. One minor issue (Leelavati sentence placement) does not affect the verdict; no material issues found.

limitations: AI editorial assessment; no observed human comprehension is claimed.
Penguin is publisher copy. It supports the book example and scope, not independent evaluation.
This review does not sign, integrate or publish the profile.
